Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1214/aop/1024404523, fetched) title 'When is the Student $t$-statistic asymptotically standard normal?', authors Evarist Gine, Friedrich Götze, David M. Mason, pages 1514-1531, print 1997-07-01. Crossref abstract (verbatim, saved /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify32h-L07-L08/cr/crossref_abstracts.json): 'Let X, X_i, i in N, be independent, identically distributed random variables. It is shown that the Student t-statistic based upon the sample {X_i} is asymptotically N(0,1) if and only if X is in the domain of attraction of the normal law.' Scope check: the abstract states no mean-zero condition. A later restatement by Mason and Shao (2001), Annals of Probability 29(4) 1435-1450, doi 10.1214/aop/1015345757 (Crossref abstract, read): 'Giné, Götze and Mason (1997) proved that T_n converges in distribution to a standard normal random variable if and only if X is in the domain of attraction of a normal random variable and EX = 0.' So the GGM result carries EX = 0. The span does not state it, but both places it appears follow an explicit zero-Sharpe-ratio sentence in the same paragraph (Remark 2.9: 'If SR = 0 and the variance is finite ...'; section 7: 'At a zero Sharpe ratio the statistic is a Student t-statistic, which ...'), so the mean-zero condition is supplied in context. PASS on scope; the statement is recorded in the registry flag as a precision note. Attribution and grade rows below. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5 (line 272): containment, monotone expected maximum, and the null-win statement
rows.evidence: unchanged since 3e8fe81 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Re-derived. Let Q_N be the maximum of N null statistics and X_N the new null. Q_N = max(Q_(N-1), X_N) >= Q_(N-1) pointwise, for any joint law of the statistics. (a) E[Q_N] >= E[Q_(N-1)]: the expected maximum cannot fall as N grows. (b) {Z + delta > Q_N} is a subset of {Z + delta > Q_(N-1)}, so the probability that the genuine configuration wins cannot rise (containment, the T span that was already at 584f614). (c) The complement: P(some null beats the genuine) = 1 - P(genuine wins) cannot fall, so 'the null configurations win at least as often' (T). Bound: Lesson 1 Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82) states 'Let Z_1, ..., Z_N each have the standard normal distribution, with any joint distribution, and N >= 2. Then E[max Z_n] <= sqrt(2 ln N)'; its proof (Jensen, e^(lambda E M) <= sum E e^(lambda Z_n) = N e^(lambda^2/2), then lambda = sqrt(2 ln N)) is re-derived and holds with no independence. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/l08_sec5_monotone.py, seed 777, 60,000 draws, N up to 60; output out_l08_sec5_monotone.txt): E[max] of the first N is non-decreasing in N for an equicorrelated law (rho 0.9), independent normals, a comonotone law and a block-random law; at every N it lies below sqrt(2 ln N) (smallest margins 0.9973, 0.5416, 1.1820 and 0.5990); P(genuine wins) with k nulls, k = 1..39, is non-increasing (0.8778, 0.8185, 0.7111, 0.6612, 0.5417, ... ). All checks pass. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5, T span (line 272): 'The luck, the expected maximum of the nulls, cannot fall as N grows, because adding a null can only raise the maximum; for standard normal null statistics with any joint law it is at most sqrt(2 ln N) (Lesson 1, Theorem 2.1)'
rows.evidence: unchanged since 3e8fe81 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Re-derived at d10fb51. Monotonicity: with N+1 nulls the maximum is the pointwise maximum over N nulls and one more variable, so it is at least the N-null maximum for every outcome, and its expectation cannot fall. Bound: for any joint law of Z_1..Z_N standard normal, e^{lambda E max Z_n} <= E e^{lambda max Z_n} (Jensen) <= sum_n E e^{lambda Z_n} = N e^{lambda^2/2}, so E max Z_n <= ln N / lambda + lambda/2 for every lambda > 0; lambda = sqrt(2 ln N) gives sqrt(2 ln N). The statement matches Lesson 1, Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82), whose scope is 'any joint distribution', and the L08 claim uses no wider scope. The index is the page's N (configurations), and the claim uses the N-1 nulls, with sqrt(2 ln(N-1)) <= sqrt(2 ln N). Concept link to L01 def-expected-maximum-sharpe exists (check_dag PASS). Card S7-c227 now covers it (L08-sec5-expected-max-card-gap). rows.evidence: unchanged since 3e8fe81 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Claim: adding a null trial cannot raise the probability that a genuine configuration wins in sample, whatever the joint law. Proof (re-derived): let X0 be the genuine in-sample statistic and M_k the maximum of k null statistics. The winning event with k nulls is {X0 > M_k}; adding a null Y gives {X0 > max(M_k, Y)}, which is contained in {X0 > M_k}, so its probability cannot exceed the earlier one. No independence or distributional assumption is used. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/spot_checks.py, 400,000 draws, a common-factor joint law, N-1 = 0,1,4,9,39 nulls): the win probability is non-increasing at every size (for example 0.6448 -> 0.4817 when a second null is added, 0.0513 -> 0.0502 at 39 nulls). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Remark 2.9 (line 204): T span 'If SR = 0 and the variance is finite, sqrt(T) SR-hat = (sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma)(sigma/sigma-hat) -> N(0,1), by the CLT for mu-hat, the LLN for sigma-hat and Slutsky's lemma'
rows.evidence: unchanged since 3e8fe81 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Derivation re-checked step by step. (i) SR-hat = mu-hat/sigma-hat, so sqrt(T) SR-hat = (sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma)(sigma/sigma-hat) is an identity. (ii) With iid returns, mean mu = SR sigma = 0 and finite variance sigma^2, the CLT gives sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma -> N(0,1). (iii) sigma-hat^2 = (1/(T-1)) sum (r - r-bar)^2 -> sigma^2 in probability by the LLN applied to r^2 (finite since E r^2 < infinity) and r-bar -> 0; so sigma/sigma-hat -> 1 in probability (the divisor T or T-1 does not matter). (iv) Slutsky gives the limit N(0,1). Nothing beyond finite variance is used. Numerical spot check (scratch num_checks.py, 20000 replications): Student t with 3 df scaled to unit variance, SR = 0: P(z <= -1.6449) = 0.0513 / 0.0502 / 0.0502 and P(z <= 1.6449) = 0.9505 / 0.9500 / 0.9506 at T = 250 / 1000 / 4000 (N(0,1): 0.05 and 0.95); sd(z) = 1.007 / 1.001 / 0.992. The fourth moment is infinite there, so the check is of the claim's sufficiency. Grade T is right (proved on the page). The iid standing assumption is the section 1 assumption ('keep independence'). rows.evidence: unchanged since 3e8fe81 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Re-graded at 50d202e. The block title is T and the block carries a complete proof on the page (Theorem 5.1 plus Slutsky, then the joint-normal sign argument), so T is right; no cite is owed. Re-derived: the naive statistic has limit N(0, theta/(V1+V2)), so the two-sided rejection limit is 2(1 - Phi(z sqrt((V1+V2)/theta))), which is below alpha iff theta < V1+V2. Under SR1 = SR2 = SR and joint normality (5) gives theta = 2(1-rho) + SR^2(1-rho^2) and V1+V2 = 2 + SR^2, so (V1+V2) - theta = rho(2 + SR^2 rho). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Corollary 5.2 (line 405-410), Proposition 5.4 (line 425-431), key-results rows 747-748
rows.evidence: unchanged since 3e8fe81 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: New row; re-derived and spot-checked numerically (scratch math_checks.py, output math_checks_out.txt). Influence of the Sharpe estimator for standardized return u: psi = u - (SR/2)(u^2 - 1); Var psi = 1 + SR^2/2; Cov(psi1, psi2) = rho + SR1 SR2 rho^2 / 2 (Isserlis: E[u1 u2] = rho, E[u1 u2^2] = 0, E[u1^2 u2^2] = 1 + 2 rho^2). Hence theta = Var(psi1 - psi2) = 2(1 - rho) + (SR1^2 + SR2^2)/2 - SR1 SR2 rho^2, the Corollary 5.2 formula (row 747). Monte Carlo with 4,000,000 draws for SR pairs (0.05,0.05), (0.1,0.3), (0.5,1.0) and rho in {-0.9,-0.5,0,0.5,0.9}: largest |MC - closed form| = 0.0035, consistent with MC error. Sign check (common SR in {0.05, 0.5, 1.3, 1.41}, rho in +-{0.1, 0.5, 0.99}): sign(theta - (V1+V2)) = -sign(rho) for every point. So Proposition 5.4's "undersized under positive correlation, oversized under negative" holds for SR^2 < 2. The limit (line 427) follows from Theorem 5.1, sqrt((T-1)/T) -> 1 and Slutsky's lemma, as the proof on lines 433-436 states; the proof's identity (V1+V2) - theta = rho(2 + SR^2 rho) (line 436) matches the derivation above. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html line 95 (C span, data-cite bailey2016probability, no locator): 'Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu introduce CSCV as one way to estimate PBO and find, in their own test cases, that it produces reasonable estimates'
rows.evidence: unchanged since 3e8fe81 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Re-checked from scratch at f14987f. Attribution (VERIFIER 2.1): the publisher abstract of Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu, The Journal of Computational Finance 20(4) (first published 19 Sep 2016; DOI 10.21314/JCF.2016.322), read on Risk.net with curl -sSL https://www.risk.net/node/2471206 (HTTP 200, 128,762 bytes; final URL https://www.risk.net/journal-of-computational-finance/2471206/the-probability-of-backtest-overfitting). It reads: 'We propose a general framework to assess the probability of backtest overfitting (PBO) ... we call these implementations combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV). We show that CSCV produces reasonable estimates of PBO for several useful examples.' The 'Need to know' summary reads: 'Results indicate that CSCV provides reasonable estimates of PBO, with relatively small errors.' The span's claim is what the abstract shows: CSCV is introduced as one way to estimate PBO, and the reasonable estimates are for 'several useful examples' that are the authors' own test cases. Scope is correct. Crossref (curl https://api.crossref.org/works/10.21314/jcf.2016.322) carries no abstract; its title, authors and year match the registry record. Grade: C is correct under BLUEPRINT §3 (single-study evidence from the authors' own examples; the venue is peer-reviewed but nothing replicates the result). Counter-evidence: no named published source contests it (row counter-bailey2016probability). The registry-scoped sentence 'No independent study in the registry has yet evaluated its accuracy' is true: a title scan of references/references.json (557 entries; pattern backtest|overfit|PBO|CSCV|combinatorial|selection bias|data snooping|cross-validation) returns 11 titles, none of which names CSCV. Apart from the source of the claim itself (bailey2016probability, which reports the authors' own examples), none of the 11 evaluates CSCV's estimates (bailey2014deflated, bailey2014pseudo, harvey2015backtesting, romano2005stepwise, white2000reality and others are about selection or snooping, not CSCV). Result: PASS.

Title 'Endogeneity and moments in time series momentum’s predictability test'; authors Lei Jiang, Liang Peng, Zhongling Qin, Bingduo Yang; The Annals of Applied Statistics 19(1), 701–719; issued 2025-03-01; publisher Institute of Mathematical Statistics. Registry record (references/references.json, entry added at 3e8fe81) gives the same title, authors, year, container, volume 19, issue 1, pages 701-719 and publisher; verify_refs checks in r23-cmd-verify_refs-unit-S7 and r23-cmd-verify_refs-offline pass. Abstract, verbatim from Crossref (JATS tags removed): 'The predictability test is critical in developing momentum trading strategies. In time-series momentum (TSM) tests via linear predictive regressions, the classical and Newey–West t-tests have size distortions because of endogeneity and a lack of enough finite moments. To tackle these issues, this paper proposes a new test that features a model of the error correlations, weighted least squares estimation, and the random weighted bootstrap method. Simulations confirm its accurate size and good power. Empirically, we revisit the evidence in (J. Financ. Econ. 135 (2020) 774–794) and find that the TSM predictability detected by the new test is much more widespread than that by the Newey–West t-tests.' Econ. 135 (2020) 774–794)', which is Huang, Li, Wang and Zhou (registry huang2020time: JFE 135(3) 774–794, the same volume and pages); 'a test that corrects the size distortions of the classical and Newey–West t-tests' paraphrases 'the classical and Newey–West t-tests have size distortions ... To tackle these issues, this paper proposes a new test ... Simulations confirm its accurate size'. 'corrects' is a fair one-word gloss of 'tackle' plus the authors' simulated 'accurate size'; the simulation basis is the paper's own, so it sits under the B grade of the span; 'much more widespread than the Newey–West tests detect' is 'much more widespread than that by the Newey–West t-tests'. rows.evidence: unchanged since 3e8fe81 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Re-derivation: under iid rows and exchangeable columns the winner's out-of-sample rank among N configurations is uniform on {1..N} (ties have probability zero for continuous draws), so logit(ω) ≤ 0 iff rank ≤ (N+1)/2, and P(logit ≤ 0) = floor((N+1)/2)/N (N even: N/2 ranks of N; N odd: (N+1)/2 ranks of N). Numerical check (scratch/r23/pbo_odd_n_sim.py; seed 20261021; 4000 draws per N; 8 rows, 4 blocks; the twin's pbo): N=2 theorem 0.5000, twin 0.4992 (se 0.0058); N=3 theorem 0.6667, twin 0.6583 (se 0.0055); N=4 theorem 0.5000, twin 0.4989 (se 0.0048); N=5 theorem 0.6000, twin 0.5985 (se 0.0048). The twin's convention (logit ≤ 0) is the one the theorem needs for odd N; the convention logit < 0 would give 0.3315 at N=3 and 0.3944 at N=5 (same script). Lab 3's trial counts are 2, 20 and 200 (even), so the lab cannot tell the two conventions apart. The gap is recorded as a surviving mutant (FAIL row mut-L08-3-tie-convention-odd-N). rows.check: 2.4-math / 2.5-lab (docstring claim re-derived; wording of the new test)
rows.location: tests/test_labs.py docstring of test_l08_lab3_pbo_counts_the_median_rank_as_overfit, lines 167-169
rows.evidence: Docstring sentence: 'Lab 3 runs 2, 20 and 200 configurations, an even count, where the selected one can never sit at the median out of sample, so its logit is never exactly 0.' Stated as a general fact it is false. With a tie, the average rank of the selected configuration can equal the median: for N = 2 and equal out-of-sample metrics the twin's rank formula gives 1 + 0 + 0.5 x (2 - 1) = 1.5, omega = 1.5/3 = 0.5, logit 0. What is true is that without tied out-of-sample metrics an integer rank cannot sit at the median of an even count. Lab 3's own draws have no ties: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify59h-L07-L08/r24/lab3_ties.py repeats the lab's seeded draws (default_rng(88), trials 2, 20, 200, 16 samples each, 8 blocks, 70 splits per sample) and reports 'splits checked: 3360 | splits with any tied OOS Sharpe ratio: 0 | splits with any tied IS Sharpe ratio: 0' (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify59h-L07-L08/r24/lab3_ties_out.txt). The test's conclusion is right; the docstring's generality is not. Severity: wording only; no test result changes (the same two node ids pass after the fix, see r24-cmd-fix-docstring).
